title: Career information about work-life balance is distributed differently by student gender and shapes career intentions
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35750, preregistered field experiment connecting college students to 10,000 working professionals
geography: United States; college students seeking career information and working professionals responding to randomized messages

observations.period: Field experiment and information intervention; paper issued September 14, 2026

denominator.unit: working professionals approached in the large-scale field experiment; student denominator and response counts may differ

information_treatment.value: professional receives a message from a male or female college student
information_treatment.unit: randomized requester-gender signal in career-information exchange

work_life_balance_information.value: female students receive substantially more information about work-life balance than male students when asking broadly about a career
work_life_balance_information.unit: gender difference in career information received

specific_question_persistence.value: the gender difference persists when students specifically ask about work-life balance
specific_question_persistence.unit: information response conditional on explicit request

career_intentions.value: information gaps are consequential for gender gaps in career intentions
career_intentions.unit: career-intention pathway following information and intervention evidence

professional_motives.value: survey evidence suggests non-altruistic motives for discussing work-life balance with women

observations.method: Large-scale field experiment randomizing whether working professionals receive a career-information message from a male or female college student, combined with an information intervention and a survey of professionals' motives.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a working paper and the abstract does not disclose the exact student sample, response rate, information-intervention design, or persistence into actual education, occupation, earnings, or work-life outcomes. Career intentions are not realized careers or household wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: Male and female college students, working professionals, broad versus explicit work-life-balance questions, career fields, and professional characteristics; effects may vary by field, identity, and labor-market context.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different information may reflect perceived relevance, strategic communication, social norms, or professional selection rather than deliberate discrimination. Information can alter intentions without improving access, work conditions, or care compatibility; the survey motive evidence does not identify every mechanism in the field exchange.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER DOI identifies the working paper.

boundary: This record establishes a gendered career-information and intention pathway in a field experiment. It does not establish realized occupation, earnings, work-life balance, care burden, discrimination, household security, or universal transfer across fields and institutions.
